title: Medleys and the long waltz sign-off at Biloxi
summary: DeDroit describes medleys, waltz sign-offs and a free morning dance at the Biloxi pavilion requiring neckties.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Did you used to connect the tunes to some of the Society orchestras today? They just, they start a beat up, like Lester Lannan, say, and they just take a whole bunch of tunes, they have it all rehearsed and everything, and they go from one thing to the other with just a little kind of an interlude- Modulation. Modulation, or, and change you out a little bit so that people don't get bored with the same key. Yeah. And then they keep going on for a long time like that. Did you used to play a tune and stop and start another one, or did you keep the same beat a long time?

Well, no. We would play an arrangement on a tune. It was only the hackney tunes. I mean, the tunes that were so well known, we'd play from one to the other. We'd play a medley. And if it was the tune that we didn't care too much about, we'd put it in a medley. See? And we used to play mostly waltz medleys. Unless like, oh, like when you want to sign off, you might want to sign off for the waltz. To Night Sweetheart or something? Yeah, well I had a medley, but the bands used to call Steal It. Down there, it had to change all the time. You know, I used to, you see over in Biloxi they'd be sitting in the chorus and you should see, but when the dancers break out they wanted to give the appearance and walk out the pavilion. You know what I mean? So I had to play a long sign off. So I used to throw them, show me the way to go home. And all the guys, all the people, they were all coming back and, show me the way to go home. You know? I played a couple of choruses and I'd say, good night ladies. And I played just about four balls on the horse field. And I said, that's all, good night folks, glad you came. But everybody knew me. I played for everybody, my friends. We played a morning dance from 11 to 12. It was free for the public. We could get all the young people over. Where was this? Biloxi. The only stipulation was that they had to wear a necktie. So some of them wouldn't have a necktie. They wouldn't let them in the pavilion. So I bought me a dozen, ten cents a necktie. I said, well, wait, put them on my trumpet case. I see a friend of mine, I want him a tie, and he put it on, he'd come in the pavilion.
